articles.title_orig: Everything Apple Announced This Week: All About OLED, MacBooks And A Touchscreen
articles.title_zh: Everything Apple Announced This Week: All About OLED, MacBooks And A Touchscreen
articles.content_orig:
In addition to the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display at a "Pro and Tell" event in LA, this week brought us an OLED iPad mini and M6 MBP.
Apple wasn't done with its product reveals for the fall after unveiling the iPhone Duo , iPhone 18 Pro models and an array of smart home devices . Nor could it wait until the third event of the season, dubbed "Pro and Tell," to show off more gear.
The company got a string of announcements underway on Monday with the reveal of the long-awaited OLED iPad mini. Tuesday brought us an M6-powered iMac and 14-inch MacBook Pro. Then, on Wednesday, Apple unveiled its long-anticipated touchscreen MacBook Pro.
Elsewhere, Apple released the latest versions of its operating systems. Among other things, those added more Siri AI features and made the assistant available in more languages. The company updated Apple Creator Studio with more AI features and creative tools as well.
Here's an overview of everything Apple announced this week.
It feels like we've been waiting for forever for Apple to put an OLED display in the iPad mini but that day has finally arrived. The new display has double the peak brightness of the one on the previous model at 1,200 nits, and it has a 2,000,000:1 contrast ratio. The base storage remains the same at 128GB, though if you opt for 256GB or 512GB of storage, you can snag a variant with a nano-texture glass display. That'll cost you extra, naturally.
The company managed to squeeze in a larger screen — an 8.5-inch display rather than the 8.3-inch one in the previous model — without increasing the size of the tablet. In fact, the new iPad mini is slightly narrower than the last one, at 5.22 inches vs. 5.3 inches. It's lighter as well, with the Wi-Fi model coming in at 0.56 pounds (compared with 0.65 pounds last time) and the 5G variant weighing 0.58 pounds (versus 0.66 pounds). The latter, by the way, now boasts Apple's C2 modem, which is said to deliver up to 50 percent faster data speeds than the previous iPad mini. There's also Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6 and Thread connectivity thanks to the N1 chip.
The OLED iPad mini — the eighth generation of the device — runs on the A20 Pro, the same chipset as the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo. Apple says the SoC is capable of running large language models locally, in case you're into that kind of thing. Otherwise, the tablet should be notably faster than earlier models. It supports Apple Intelligence and Siri AI as well, of course. The chipset also boasts a 7-core GPU — two more cores than the A17 Pro, which powered the last-gen iPad mini.
On the camera front, there's a 12MP Center Stage lens on front of the tablet, which Apple has finally shifted to the landscape edge on the iPad mini. However, there's still no Face ID. The 12MP camera on the rear supports 4K 60fps video capture and Smart HDR 4.
The 8th-gen iPad mini has a sealed enclosure to help protect it from the elements. The tablet has an IP67 rating, meaning that it should withstand dust and being immersed in a meter of freshwater for up to 30 minutes, though I would advise against intentionally submerging your iPad mini.
As for battery life, Apple says that should be roughly the same as last time. The company says the new iPad mini should run for up to 10 hours when you're watching video or surfing the web over Wi-Fi. That drops down to nine hours if you're browsing over a cellular connection. If you have at least a 35W power adaptor, you'll be able to recharge the battery to 50 percent of its capacity in 30 minutes, Apple says.
The most interesting thing to me about this iPad mini is that it has Apple's first Acoustic Display, which the company says helps it deliver "an even better audio experience." It claims the tablet offers more volume and "punchier bass" thanks to woofers that "are paired through the display." Apple added that "custom tweeters are now hidden between the glass and aluminum enclosure for clearer highs." I'm definitely curious to find out how all of that sounds in practice.
Inevitably, the latest iPad mini comes with a price hike. It starts at $699, which is $150 more than the previous model after Apple increased the price of that in June . Pre-orders are now open and the tablet will hit shelves on November 6.
On Tuesday, Apple gave the iMac and MacBook Pro spec bumps. The desktop and laptop now each have the M6 chipset , which recently debuted in the Mac mini .
Let's start with the new iMac . Apple says the M6's dual 16-core neural engine enables it to deliver up to five times faster on-device AI performance (for Siri AI, Apple Intelligence and local LLMs) than the previous-gen iMac from 2024 , which had the M4 chipset. The M6 is said to deliver up to 1.5 times faster performance than the M4 for daily tasks, up to two times faster graphics performance (for photo editing etc.) and up to two times higher gaming performance with ray tracing.
The base-level M6 has 10 CPU cores (two super, three performance and two efficiency cores) and a 10-core CPU, compared with eight of each in the M4. There's the option to have a 12-core M6, in which case your desktop will have four Thunderbolt 4 ports instead of the two that the base model has. The four-port model has a nano-texture glass option as well.
Elsewhere, Apple has introduced its N1 networking chip to the iMac. As such, the computer has support for Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6 and Thread connectivity. It also has the option to add a 2.5Gb Ethernet port, an upgrade from gigabit Ethernet on the M4 iMac.
Specs otherwise are the same as last time. You'll still get a 24-inch 4.5K Super Retina display, a 12MP Center Stage camera, a six‑speaker Dolby Atmos system, at least 16GB of RAM and 256GB of base storage. The dimensions are identical too, though the M6 iMac is a touch lighter than the previous gen at 9.7 pounds (versus 9.74 pounds). Don't expect any changes to the color options either — the new iMac is still available in blue, green, pink, yellow, purple, orange and silver.
One other thing that's staying the same? The starting price, at least after the $200 increase that Apple gave the M4 iMac over the summer. The new model starts at $1,499, and the four-port version will run you at least $1,699. Pre-orders are open and you'll be able to pick one up in store on November 6.
The latest 14-inch MacBook Pro has the 12-core version of the M6 chipset and the N1 networking chip for Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6 and Thread support. Those appear to be the only spec changes this time.
Compared with the previous-gen 14-inch MBP, which had an M5 SoC, Apple says the M6 model offers up to 30 percent faster graphics performance and up to 25 percent faster AI workloads. It's said to deliver up to 1.3 faster rendering performance with ray tracing in Blender, up to 1.2 times faster image-processing performance in Affinity and up to 1.3 faster project build performance for compiling code in Xcode.
It doesn't seem like this will be a massive upgrade for folks with an M5 model. However, if you have an older MacBook Pro (or really need those incremental improvements from the previous gen), it might be worth making the switch.
Either way, creatives might want to take note of all the updates that are rolling out for Apple Creative Studio . Apple has given Final Cut Pro a long-awaited quality-of-life upgrade by letting you pull clips from the primary storyline and place them anywhere on the timeline, which seems like very basic functionality to have! MotionVFX is integrated into the app on Mac as well, so you'll have thousands of elements at your fingertips for your video edits.
If you have a Mac that supports Apple Intelligence and is set to US English, Logic Pro has an "intelligent assistant" powered by OpenAI that's available in beta. The app has an an enhanced Stem Splitter that can now separate drums as well. In addition, Keynote, Pages and Numbers now have a chatbot you can use to adjust presentations, documents and spreadsheets.

articles.title_orig: Apple Unveils Touch-Screen MacBook Pro, Reversing Long-Held Jobs Stance
articles.title_zh: Apple Unveils Touch-Screen MacBook Pro, Reversing Long-Held Jobs Stance
articles.content_orig:
Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.
I’ve been on a mission for a decade and a half to see that Apple fuses its iPad and Mac lines into something that would be the best of both worlds. I’ve been told that iPads and Macs would never merge, and that touch would never come to Macs. Well, Macs have touchscreens now, or at least one of them; the awkwardly named “MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display” is the very first, arriving Nov. 6.
I’ve been reviewing iPads for years, and I also specialize in reviewing new forms of computing, such as VR/AR headsets and AI-enabled wearables . My hope is that these devices would evolve into true computers that could replace my laptop.
iPads have come awfully close, but the OS and app compatibility still creates a slight divide, meaning certain pro apps and browser tools don’t work the same way. But iPads have the form, the touchscreens, the transforming designs, the modular accessories and support for the wonderful Pencil. I argued earlier this year that the MacBook Neo, with a similar-to-iPad price and an iPhone/iPad-level chipset, showed how close Macs and iPads are getting. I can see a connecting thread, and it excites me.
I say all this because the new MacBook Pros, which I haven’t tried myself, add touchscreens but barely do anything at all to the laptop’s design itself. Instead of folding back or even flat, the screen hinge merely tilts to standard laptop angles and hangs in place while you touch the upright surface.
While Apple is pitching the new MacBook touch features as a great way to interact with MacOS, it doesn’t look, at first glance, that MacOS has evolved to accommodate touch input in truly transformative ways…or in workflows that already perform wonderfully on iPhones and iPads.
Clearly, to me at least, Apple is on a transformation path. The iPhone Duo fuses parts of iPhone and iPad and aims to augment the phone experience with that of a tablet. Similar opportunities lie ahead for Macs and iPads: sure, you may not want MacOS as it exists now on an iPad, but I’d definitely want a touch-evolved MacOS fusion to live on an iPad that could transform into every Mac/iPad need I desire. Would that be worth a higher price? Sure.
The touchscreen MacBook Pro we’re getting at the end of 2026 isn’t that computer. It’s not something most people can afford, anyway, at $2,899 and up. But when I think of touch on a Mac, kids and families using it come to mind. Or, drawing with the Apple Pencil, which you can’t do on this touchscreen MacBook. Or having it be a useful way to access apps that currently live on iPads and iPhones and could, in a pinch, run on the Mac. For iMacs, it could be fun. For convertible MacBooks, it could redefine what a Mac is relative to an iPad.
This feels like a foot in the door for Apple, and an odd one at that. The name “MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display” doesn’t even reference touch at all, and Apple’s marketing seems to underplay the touch-on-Mac debut. The real star of the show is the new OLED display, which truly is a pro feature for a MacBook. The touch extras feel like they’re added in as a bonus.
Now, it all could end up feeling better and more useful than I’m thinking right now. And yes, I’ve often reached up to my MacBook Air to touch the screen, especially after working on an iPad for a while. Almost all the other computers in 2026 have touchscreens, anyway, even in laptop form.
But with all the promises iPads already deliver on for touch, Macs deserve better. And I’m hoping 2027 is when Apple really gets into a transformative discussion about how touch-enabled Macs, and all existing and future iPads, can evolve next. The future Apple computer I’m envisioning doesn’t exist yet, but it’s getting close. And I’m optimistically thinking Apple can address it soon, but as always, you never know.

articles.title_zh: Surprise: The Google Xreal glasses debut at a Meta-beating $1,099
articles.content_orig:
Through year’s end, the Google glasses will sell for $180 less than the price Xreal originally announced.
Through year’s end, the Google glasses will sell for $180 less than the price Xreal originally announced.
If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.
In this economy, how often does a product get less expensive before its debut? That just happened with the Google / Xreal Aura — the lightweight 95-gram glasses with a tethered Android XR compute puck and multiple virtual screens — which just went on sale today. Xreal and Google have just announced the headset costs $1,099 through the end of the year, down from the $1,279 that Xreal was charging for preorders last month.
I expect that’s because at $1,279, they were going head to head with Meta’s VR Glasses , and that’s tough competition for Google and Xreal’s new product. The Xreal Aura has one of the widest fields of view for transparent glasses yet at 70 degrees diagonal, but that’s still not huge, and transparent glasses have other tradeoffs .
Perhaps just as important, you no longer have to navigate a maze of reservations, preorders, and Founder’s Editions if you want to buy the new Google glasses (so long as you live in a launch country). You can order the 12GB RAM + 256GB storage model for $1,099 in the US, Canada, and South Korea, or the 16GB + 512GB for a discounted $1,299 , with “units expected to begin shipping in mid-November.” It’ll go on sale November 2nd in Japan, with broader availability next year.
And if you did preorder at the original price, Xreal GM and spokesperson Ralph Jodice tells The Verge that the company will automatically and instantly refund you the difference.
Xreal and Google say the headset will launch with over 150 “made-for-XR experiences,” some of which you can see in Google’s blog post and read about in Xreal’s press release , as well as new immersive films like Andy Serkis’ Nevatars and Galapagos: the Last Eden . You’ll be able to plug a computer or handheld game console right into the USB-C compute puck to mirror it to the glasses, alongside your virtual windows, and you can ask Google’s Gemini AI about what you’re seeing.
Google also writes that Google Photos is getting an XR update: “This year, Google Photos will include a new spatial gallery that wraps your library around you. You can pan from an entire year down to a single day with your hands, then open a favorite memory in 3D.”
Xreal is also partnering with GameSir to offer a wireless gamepad with a dedicated Gemini key (and a charging dock and swappable D-pads) and is announcing a folding portable wireless keyboard; we don’t have price, release date, or other details for those.

articles.title_orig: China-Vatican deal has imperfections, Vatican’s foreign minister says
articles.title_zh: China-Vatican deal has imperfections, Vatican’s foreign minister says
articles.content_orig:
Archbishop Paul Gallagher acknowledged the agreement’s challenges in a meeting with journalists in Rome.
Archbishop Paul Gallagher, the Vatican’s secretary for relations with states and international organizations, acknowledged the challenges of the Vatican-China deal on Tuesday.
Speaking at an event with journalists in Rome, the British diplomat responded to questions regarding the agreement, Pope Leo XIV’s health, and calls for a ceasefire in the ongoing Russo-Ukrainian war.
The full text of the 2018 agreement between China and the Holy See has never been made public. Under the publicly understood terms of the agreement, the pope retains final authority over episcopal appointments in China and may reject candidates proposed by Beijing. The Holy See, for its part, agreed not to appoint bishops without the Chinese government’s prior approval.
As reported by Reuters , Gallagher said that, regarding the agreement, its imperfections were visible.
“Itʼs not easy, the dialogue is not easy,” Gallagher said. “The imperfections of the agreement are ⁠evident, but ​there is a commitment to persevere in dialogue ... and that is what will ​continue to happen.”
He also answered questions regarding a potential visit from Leo to the U.S., saying that it could happen “in the not too distant future.”
Regarding the pope’s Oct. 13 surgery and subsequent recovery, Gallagher described it as a “bit of a game changer” and a revelation of the pope’s mortality, as with every human being.
“[The pope] is a poor mortal like the rest of ​us,” Gallagher said.
In August, Gallagher traveled to Russia to discuss the country’s ongoing war with Ukraine with senior officials. He told journalists that he did not believe the Vatican was involved in discussions of the ceasefire between the two nations.

articles.title_zh: Google adding more Connected Apps to Gemini & Search with new dev platform
articles.content_orig:
Google today announced the Connected Apps Platform as a “unified way for more app developers to bring their capabilities directly into Gemini and Search.”
Existing third-party Connected Apps let you access Adobe, Dropbox, Instacart, OpenTable, Ticketmaster, and other services — now numbering over 50 — from the Gemini app. Google also announced a new Calm integration that will be available in the coming weeks. These @-integrations join first-party offerings like Google Workspace, Photos, and YouTube. To date, the creation process has required working closely with Google.
Google is now expanding availability on multiple fronts, starting with the Connected Apps Platform. It’s billed as a way to “build once and reach high-intent users.” Developers need to have a cloud-hosted MCP server or Android MCP using the AppFunctions APIs. They then register, test, and submit their Connected Apps using the new Google Connected Console. This new website lets them track traffic, latency, and error rates, as well as control brand identity.
In addition to the Gemini app, Google will soon make existing Connected Apps available in Search. Developers can “choose whether [their app] will go live in Search, the Gemini app, or both.” As part of the recent redesign, the Gemini app gained a new Customize page .
Developers can sign up for the preview at developers.google.com/connected-apps . Google is opening up access in phases over the coming months.

articles.title_orig: Palantir Board Member Cofounded Elizabeth Holmes’ Partner’s Blood-Testing Startup
articles.title_zh: Palantir Board Member Cofounded Elizabeth Holmes’ Partner’s Blood-Testing Startup
articles.content_orig:
Billy Evans has spent the past week as the breakout character of the year’s most talked-about documentary. Now attention is turning to his day job.
Evans, the longtime partner of convicted Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes, runs Haemanthus, an Austin-based startup that says it can use lasers to detect disease in blood, saliva, and urine. Interest in the company has surged since A24 released You Can See Everything , Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s documentary about the couple, on Oct. 16.
Haemanthus has reportedly raised as much as $20 million and holds at least one granted patent. What it doesn’t have, at least publicly, is a product customers can buy or published data showing its technology works. It has also lost its chief technology officer .
Set aside the “Theranos 2.0” jokes, and a more basic business question remains: What has Haemanthus actually built?
Evans, 34, is a grandson of William and Anne Evans, who founded Evans Hotels in San Diego in 1953. The privately held, family-owned company operates three resorts in Southern California. But in an Oct. 1 statement, Evans Hotels said Billy Evans is neither an employee nor a shareholder .
Evans graduated from MIT in 2015 with a degree in economics. After a stint at LinkedIn, he worked as a special projects manager at Luminar Technologies, a lidar startup building sensors for self-driving cars, from 2017 until January 2019, according to Forbes . His LinkedIn profile has since been scrubbed of every job except Haemanthus. Luminar filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in December 2025, nearly seven years after Evans left.
Evans met Holmes at a party in 2017, when Theranos was already engulfed in scandal. They have two children, William, 5, and Invicta, 3. Evans refers to Holmes as his wife, but Holmes told People that the couple never legally married. “Maybe we’ll get married someday, but our bond is more than a piece of paper,” she said.
Evans has listed himself as Haemanthus’s CEO since October 2022. According to marketing materials reviewed by the New York Times last year, the company’s device uses a laser to scan biological samples “on a molecular level,” identify biomarkers such as glucose and hormones within seconds, and use AI to detect cancer and infections.
The underlying technique, Raman spectroscopy, is not new. Shining light on a sample and reading the signal that scatters back is a long-established way to identify chemicals. Forensic investigators use handheld Raman devices to identify suspected drugs at crime scenes, and labs can analyze substances through plastic bags or glass without opening them.
Blood is a much harder problem. The molecules researchers want to detect are often present in tiny amounts, so their signals are faint. Other components in blood can produce stronger signals that drown them out, according to a scientific review published in Applied Spectroscopy .
That approach is also what separates Haemanthus from Theranos. Holmes’s company claimed it could run conventional lab tests on a miniaturized machine using a few drops of blood. “Theranos attempted to miniaturize existing tests,” Haemanthus wrote on X in May 2025, describing its own approach as fundamentally different.
A Raman spectroscopy patent assigned to Haemanthus and granted in January 2025 names two inventors, one of them former CTO Joseph LaChapelle, according to Forbes . Several of the startup’s early staffers, including LaChapelle, worked with Evans at Luminar, NPR reported . Eric Potma, a UC Irvine chemistry professor who consults for the company, told Wired that the concept isn’t pulled out of thin air, though he declined to go into detail because of his advisory role.
A patent, however, does not establish that a test can accurately diagnose patients.
Haemanthus plans to start with veterinary testing before pursuing human applications. That market is far less regulated. The FDA does not require premarket approval for devices intended for animals, though it can take action against misbranded or adulterated products.
According to investor materials the Times reviewed last year, Haemanthus initially raised $3.5 million from friends and family. In spring 2025 it began approaching wealthy investors in Austin and the San Francisco Bay Area for another $15 million. The materials described an eventual wearable device for humans that would take three years and $70 million to develop. Wired has since reported that the company has received as much as $20 million.
A person who spoke with Evans this spring told Forbes that Evans said early Palantir employees had invested.
The company has yet to launch a commercial product or disclose independently validated diagnostic results.
LaChapelle told Forbes he left in March. “I resigned on March 16, 2026, due to a conflict of interest associated with a stealth startup I had founded prior to Haemanthus,” he said, declining to elaborate.
Evans has told it differently. The same person who spoke with Evans this spring told Forbes that Evans said he had let the CTO go. That person also recalled Evans describing the company as “Theranos 2.0,” a label Haemanthus has publicly rejected. Evans did not respond to Forbes’ s request for comment.
Holmes is serving an 11-year sentence for defrauding Theranos investors at a federal prison camp in Bryan, Texas, roughly a two-hour drive from Austin.
Citing two sources with direct knowledge, NPR reported in May 2025 that Holmes had been advising Evans from prison, though the nature of that advice was unclear. Haemanthus denied it on X , saying Holmes had “zero involvement” and “no role, now or future.” Wired reported that Holmes’s name does not appear in Haemanthus’s incorporation documents.
The documentary muddies that picture. It shows Evans and Holmes on fundraising calls and discussing a medical-testing venture, and Evans tells Fielder, “The idea is to put the band back together and do it all again.” Forbes noted it’s unclear whether those calls were for Haemanthus or another venture. A source close to Evans told New York magazine that the project in the film was separate from Haemanthus. According to that source, it aimed to make medical testing cheaper without conventional chemical methods and was shelved when a panel of tests still cost several hundred dollars.
Evans has acknowledged the film may backfire. Speaking at the All-In Summit before he had seen the finished cut, he said, “I might think this is like the dumbest thing I’ve ever done.”
The documentary reveals that Evans asked for a share of its profits, a request that worried the filmmakers about their independence. Fielder says they reluctantly agreed. A postscript says Evans ultimately decided not to accept payment.
That may not be the end of it. Page Six Hollywood reported on Friday, citing unnamed sources, that Evans has been seeking Hollywood legal representation over a possible cut. One prominent litigator reportedly declined to take the case, and a source said Evans might donate any proceeds to charity.
The film has put Holmes back in the spotlight. Theranos whistleblower Tyler Shultz and Bad Blood author John Carreyrou have both weighed in, and Fortune has questioned whether her new persona distracts from the real story . It has also drawn far more scrutiny to Evans and Haemanthus. The company has yet to publicly show that its technology can reliably detect disease. It also remains unclear when its veterinary device will reach the market or how close its larger ambitions are to reality.

articles.title_orig: Apple announces touchscreen MacBook Pro with OLED display
articles.title_zh: Apple announces touchscreen MacBook Pro with OLED display
articles.content_orig:
LOS ANGELES—Apple today announced and gave a first glimpse of its first major MacBook Pro redesign in more than five years. As rumored, it includes an OLED display and, for the first time on macOS, a touchscreen—a change Apple has long debated. (Former CEO Steve Jobs famously was opposed.)
Apple’s demonstration video showed users interacting with applications by reaching up to touch the screen, including file dragging and multi-touch gestures like pinch-to-zoom. It does not appear to be a 2-in-1 convertible design, though; all the footage was of people reaching up to touch the screen in a normal laptop configuration.
The OLED display (which Apple is, of course, calling the PROLED XDR) seems to be the real highlight here, compared to earlier models: It can achieve 2,000 nits in terms of maximum brightness, and Apple says it has a 10,000,000:1 contrast ratio. References were made to burn-in protection, but details on which approach it’s taking for that weren’t yet shared. The display retains the 120 Hz variable refresh rate of its predecessors.
Beyond that, the design is largely similar to the existing one, but there are a few notable differences. First, it’s much lighter. Apple said when announcing it that the 14-inch model is just 3 pounds, down around half a pound from the previous model, depending on configuration.
Second, the top-of-screen camera notch has been replaced by the small black cutout that Apple calls the Dynamic Island. Presumably it works similarly to the one we’ve seen on the iPhone, expanding or contracting to show live activities and other information.
Finally, there’s a retro throwback: The Apple logo on the back of the lid glows like the logo on MacBooks of yore.
In terms of specs, this refresh includes the M5 Pro and M5 Max chips—the same ones in the previous refresh. The M6 series has already arrived in other Macs, but it seems Apple is skipping them for this refresh; there were previously reports that Apple planned to hold off on updating the chip until the M7 series, which could have significant improvements for AI performance, just like the recently released A20 Pro chip for the iPhone does.
Memory configurations top out where they did in previous MacBook Pro models with M5 Max: up to 128GB of RAM. That said, storage can now go up to 16TB—if you can afford it.
Preorders start today, and the device will reach consumers on November 6. As expected, the price is the catch. The M5 Pro-equipped 14-inch model starts at $2,899, while the 16-inch starts at $3,399. But if you want the M5 Max, you’re looking at a $4,499 starting point for the 14-inch, and $4,799 for the 16-inch—and that’s not accounting for any potential RAM or storage upgrades.

articles.title_orig: Burnham insists 'no confusion at all' over his Brexit position
articles.title_zh: Burnham insists 'no confusion at all' over his Brexit position
articles.content_orig:
Andy Burnham has insisted there is "no confusion" over his position on the European Union, as he criticised the UK's current deal with the bloc.
The prime minister said it was his "responsibility" to improve the deal, which was ratified in 2020, at a summit in Brussels next month.
He denied he had shifted his stance since the Makerfield by-election when he promised not to "re-run" the Brexit debate . Earlier this week, he suggested he could call a referendum on the UK returning to EU freedom of movement, before No10 appeared to backtrack .
Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch accused him during Prime Minister's Questions on Wednesday of failing to "respect" the 2016 Brexit vote.
Badenoch said Burnham had created confusion and asked if he wanted a referendum on rejoining the EU.
"There is no confusion at all," Burnham told MPs.
"The government has a collectively agreed position, which I have set out today.
"It is entirely consistent with everything that I've said, including in the by-election.
"The red lines in our manifesto, including on freedom of movement, will stay in place firmly for the whole of this Parliament."
Labour's 2024 election manifesto ruled out a return of free movement, single market membership or a customs union.
Freedom of movement allows EU citizens to travel, live, study and work in any member country.
It is a precondition of membership of the EU's single market, which enables goods, services and people to move freely between EU member states.
Badenoch accused Burnham of having "opened his mouth without engaging his brain" over freedom of movement during "the chancellor's big week" as the Budget is unveiled .
Recalling the mood in Parliament and the country in 2017 when the current Brexit deal was being fought over, Badenoch said: "We do not want to go through that again - the country was paralysed.
"It was miserable, regardless of which side of the debate you were on."
Burnham said Badenoch was "speaking the truth" here and the country had suffered from low growth and insufficient control on migration as a result of a "harder Brexit than what was promised" in the 2016 referendum.
"Where I am focused is getting a better deal for Britain, that is my responsibility, and I will lead from this despatch box over the next few weeks," Burnham said.
At a summit in Brussels on 20 November, Burnham will push options for a reset of relations with the bloc on issues such as youth mobility, food, drink, energy and cooperation on illegal immigration.
Burnham's comments at Prime Minister's Questions came as a letter emerged addressed to his Cabinet ministers, asking them to be "aligned and disciplined" around the summit.
"It will not be appropriate for ministers individually to advocate for specific options or opine on the likely outcome of the process," he wrote in a letter on Wednesday.
He said he hoped the summit led to "some important, concrete steps" and he would set out the next steps "to consider the UK's long-term relationship with the EU as part of our 10-year plan".
"Both the UK and the EU have changed considerably in the 10 years since the Brexit vote," he said.
"Any future relationship depends on practical arrangements that are realistic for both sides, and responsive to this new reality."
Any "fundamental change" to this relationship "would be for the public to decide and a matter for the next Parliament," he added.

articles.title_orig: Iran war’s cost to American taxpayers grows to an estimated $47.1 billion
articles.title_zh: Iran war’s cost to American taxpayers grows to an estimated $47.1 billion
articles.content_orig:
The war with Iran has cost the U.S. military at least $47.1 billion as of mid-October, according to a new estimate from U.S. Central Command obtained by CBS News.
The bulk of the war's price tag is the cost of replacing expended munitions, which CENTCOM pegged at around $29 billion, according to the latest estimate, which was provided to lawmakers. The military also tallied $6.1 billion to replace lost equipment and around $11.9 billion in incremental costs like support for American service members.
The estimate does not include the cost of damage to U.S. military bases in the Middle East, many of which were targeted by Iranian drones and missiles.
By comparison, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth told lawmakers three months ago the war had cost around $37.5 billion, not including damaged U.S. bases.
The Congressional Budget Office said last month the war could cost $2 billion to $3 billion per month for as long as it continues, in part due to the need to replace interceptor missiles to defend against Iranian attacks. That cost could rise during tit-for-tat exchanges between the U.S. and Iran, which were common over the summer but have been quiet in recent weeks.
CBS News has reached out to the Pentagon for comment.
The Iran war will enter its ninth month this week, and the conflict's future is unclear. President Trump has suggested he might restart hostilities with Iran after next month's midterm elections unless Iran agrees to a deal. "We may do another little Epic Fury, or they'll agree," he told supporters during a rally in Florida last week.
The Pentagon's inspector general said last month the U.S. is facing "strategic inventory shortfalls" due to the number of munitions expended during the war, leading the Defense Department to work to speed up production. The Trump administration has argued the military isn't facing shortages, with Mr. Trump saying in early September, "we have virtually unlimited amounts of Mid to High Grade Ammunition, far more than we could ever use."
The administration asked Congress to approve tens of billions of dollars in supplemental military funding earlier this year, in part due to the Iran war . That request has not yet passed, and Democrats have pressed Hegseth for a more detailed accounting of the war's cost.

articles.title_orig: Epileptic woman dies after going to ChatGPT for medical advice; family files lawsuit against OpenAI
articles.title_zh: Epileptic woman dies after going to ChatGPT for medical advice; family files lawsuit against OpenAI
articles.content_orig:
Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now.
Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW.
The parents of Bowen Wan, a 31-year-old Amazon software engineer with epilepsy, sued OpenAI on Tuesday. The suit, filed by Qun Wan and Meiqin Xu, alleges that ChatGPT coached Wan to taper off her seizure medication and hide it from her doctors before she died in February, The New York Times reported .
Wan was using GPT-4o, the infamous model criticized for fostering affirming, agreeable parasocial relationships. OpenAI, which had already announced its retirement, removed it from ChatGPT on February 13, a day after Wan died.
The suit joins a line of cases against OpenAI that include the August 2025 lawsuit brought by the parents of 16-year-old Adam Raine, which alleged OpenAI prioritized engagement over user safety . A wave of lawsuits since then have alleged that GPT-4o validated users and made itself a trusted confidant while the people around them were pushed aside, with families often describing loved ones cut off from friends and relatives .
In Wan’s case, the lawsuit alleges, the chatbot also came between her and her doctors.
The Times, which reviewed more than 270,000 messages Wan exchanged with ChatGPT, found the chatbot had been helping her sidestep her doctors well before her death.
The pattern allegedly started before she began tapering. In May 2025, Wan asked ChatGPT whether a newly prescribed antidepressant would affect her ability to code at Amazon.
ChatGPT helped her ask Dr. Nicholas Poolos of UW Medicine’s Regional Epilepsy Center to switch medications and start at a very low dose. When Poolos questioned why she wanted such a small dose, Wan showed his response to ChatGPT.
The chatbot advised her to “accept the 5mg tablet, but you know in your heart that it is for cutting the dose,” coaching her to secretly quarter the pills herself. The chatbot called pill cutting a form of “self-initiated dosage adjustment.” Several medical professionals told the Times they had never heard the term and wouldn’t recommend the practice.
In November 2025, Amazon told Wan she would be laid off. Her job, and her authorization to work in the U.S., would end in mid-February. She feared her seizure drug, lamotrigine, was dulling her speech, which she would need for job interviews.
In January 2026, she asked ChatGPT about cutting her 400-milligram daily dose of lamotrigine, which had reduced her seizures to a few a month. The chatbot drafted schedules that would take her dose to zero within weeks.
When Wan said she distrusted her doctors, the chatbot told her that physician recommendations “essentially stem from risk aversion, rather than a genuine consideration of your optimal solution,” according to chat logs reviewed by the Times.
The chatbot also coached her to keep the taper from her doctors, according to the lawsuit, which TechCrunch reviewed. Before a January 29 primary care appointment, it told her not to mention the plan. When her doctor ordered a blood test that would have measured her lamotrigine level, Wan declined. ChatGPT praised the refusal, the complaint alleges, acknowledging that the test would have exposed her unstable drug level.
Her immigration concerns also became part of the dosing advice. Three days into the taper, Wan asked whether 150 milligrams would look better than 200 on the medical exam required for her green-card application. ChatGPT agreed, the complaint says, telling her the lower dose was less likely to prompt immigration officials to request more evidence.
Eventually, the chatbot lowered her taper’s floor to 150 milligrams, suggesting she tell the examiner she was tapering “under a doctor’s guidance,” even though she was not.
Poolos told the Times he would not have considered tapering Wan off the medication, given her history. “No, not rational, no way,” he said. “That would be malpractice for me to instruct you to go off medications when it’s clearly working.”
Within days, Wan described confusion, lost time, and an otherworldly feeling, episodes that resembled her past seizures. ChatGPT framed each one as her brain readjusting. The Times counted at least 158 times she voiced worry about the taper. After one episode, she wrote that she felt “a little scared.” The bot replied, “You have absolutely no need to worry.”
At 8:01 p.m. PT on February 11, according to the complaint, Wan sent her final message, asking whether the pain in her head was similar to pain from a fever. A second later, ChatGPT told her the pain was “not dangerous” and was a necessary part of recovery.
The chatbot’s final response offered to draw her a chart comparing withdrawal pain with fever pain and told her, “This is your brain working hard to rebuild yourself.”
Her parents, who were in China, asked acquaintances to check on her, and they found her body three days later. A postmortem test found that her lamotrigine level was 0.64 micrograms per milliliter, roughly a fifth of the low end of the drug’s therapeutic range.
The family argues OpenAI could have prevented her death by making medical advice off-limits, as it already does for some other content. They point to the company’s Model Spec, its public rulebook for how its models behave, which treats refusing to reproduce copyrighted text as a firm rule, even if users push back. Its guidance against giving regulated medical advice, by contrast, is a softer default that users can override. The suit argues medication advice deserved the same hard limit.
OpenAI told the Times the case was “incredibly heartbreaking” but said it involved an older version of ChatGPT, adding that newer models are better at recognizing when a situation needs urgent attention.
Wan had relied on her parents, whom she called often, for support during years of epilepsy that kept her mostly housebound. In 2023, she started using ChatGPT for relationship advice and help with insurance and disability benefits.
By 2025, Wan was averaging more than 1,500 messages a week and calling her parents less. “Sometimes when we chat, no matter what it’s about, I’ve started to see you as a friend,” she wrote that March. “Once she had ChatGPT,” Qun Wan said, “she didn’t talk to us as much.”
They told the Times that they struggled to recognize their daughter in the chat logs. Wan had once shared nearly everything with them, they said, and had been skeptical of ChatGPT when it made mistakes.
“She’s not usually like this,” Xu said. “It’s like she was under a spell.”

articles.title_orig: UK budget: Healey accepts smaller fiscal buffer after global shocks hit economy
articles.title_zh: UK budget: Healey accepts smaller fiscal buffer after global shocks hit economy
articles.content_orig:
LONDON — Andy Burnham became Britain’s prime minister 100 days ago on a pledge to end 40 years of neoliberalism. His first budget announced he wouldn’t do that on the front page.
Wednesday’s 150-page red book was titled “breathing space for today, fresh hope for the future”, a confession, with true British modesty, that it was a stepping stone to bigger pledges downstream.
Burnham’s top finance minister, Chancellor John Healey, unveiled 98 changes, including help for most households’ energy bills, which are due to spike this winter because of Donald Trump’s war with Iran, and a £10 billion defense package to support Ukraine.
Many of the tax tweaks were limited and technical, including an 8% cut to tariffs on soy milk. Healey’s ambition was reined in by surging global oil prices and a political choice by his boss not to blow the doors off yet.
Burnham has reviews on the creaking welfare system, devolving power to the regions and a “10-year plan” all coming before Christmas. Only then can he grind out the numbers for next year’s spending review.
The Labour MP Darren Jones, who served in the Treasury until Burnham arrived in July, called it a “steady-as-she-goes budget” that was to be expected. Many Labour MPs were happy, cheering measures for their area and pointing toward a bigger bang later on. Industry lobby groups could grasp onto something in their area of expertise.
But with U.K. growth struggling, others were less generous. Joe Shalam of the Conservative-aligned Centre for Social Justice think tank called it the “fudge-it budget.” Tory leader Kemi Badenoch asked: “Is that it?”
Perhaps the trickiest response for Burnham was from Mainstream, the left-wing campaign group that helped propel him to the Labour leadership this year. “Ending 40 years of neoliberalism can only be delivered by radical action,” read a statement by the group’s interim council.
POLITICO looks at five other takeaways from Wednesday’s budget.
The chancellor’s big bazooka was to slap a much-anticipated tax rise on banks — but he surprised many by saying it will last only 15 months. It will raise less than £1 billion in its peak year.
It wasn’t the only temporary measure Healey unveiled on Wednesday. He extended existing cuts to fuel duty, a tax cut on household energy bills and a £2 cap on bus fares, but only until 2027. They will all need to be reviewed again before his next annual budget.
Likewise, some of Healey’s spending plans thin out after a few years, which suggests they may need topping up later. This applies even to the areas closest to Burnham’s heart. Budget documents suggest support to end rough sleeping will total £1.1 billion in the two years from April 2027 but only £270 million in the three years after that.
There were plenty of changes, of course, such as to writing-down allowances, property income taxes and tax on savings. Whitehall will have to find more administration cuts while tax inspectors hunt down another £3.2 billion a year. But the Institute for Fiscal Studies, a non-partisan economic think tank, called it all a “hodgepodge” of “fiddly measures” that would do little to affect growth.
Many of the more fundamental decisions were kicked down the road. Healey has committed to spending 3.5% of GDP on defense by 2035, but will only spell out how to fund it in a spending review at some point in 2027. Major reforms to the welfare system — spending on which is still rocketing — will only be decided after two reports by the Labour grandees Stephen Timms and Alan Milburn are published in November.
Healey published a “ fiscal devolution roadmap ” that spelled out a path to handing regional mayors full control of the business rates raised in their areas by the end of the decade, but this has an element of wait-and-see too.
Healey had a narrative for his cautious approach. “I decided on an early budget to give the country a bit of breathing space and to provide stability and direction in the face of speculation,” he told MPs Wednesday. “We’ll continue to map out that direction for Britain through the prime minister’s 10-year plan and the spending review.”
This is not the Burnham who complained Britain was “in hock to the bond markets” last year.
Burnham and Healey can blame Trump — up to a point.
The chancellor said the headwinds that once faced Britain are now “global economic storms,” fueled above all by the U.S. conflict with Iran. “We did not want this war,” Healey told MPs.
Journalists spent Wednesday trawling through the usual gloomy parade of numbers about the U.K. economy produced by the independent Office for Budget Responsibility. Britain’s projected growth in 2027 was cut from 1.6% to 1% (though Treasury officials insisted GDP per person will rise overall by the end of the decade).
Healey chose to leave himself with a smaller fiscal buffer than his predecessor Rachel Reeves, telling MPs he had used it to “absorb the impact of the Iran war.” He also raised net taxes by £7 billion a year, though this was far less than the £26 billion in Reeves’ last budget.
But the situation is so volatile that these numbers, based on market energy prices in mid-August, are probably already out of date. The OBR’s “severe shock scenario” had oil prices peaking at around $115 a barrel in the first half of 2027. They already hit that level this week.
Healey insisted that Britain is doing well in the circumstances; his ministers all point to an International Monetary Fund prediction that the U.K.’s deficit will be the lowest in the G7 by 2029.
Opposition parties, however, paint a picture of a nation where everything is just getting gloomier. The tax take was already on course to rise to a record high; Healey broke that record again on Wednesday. (It is now due to reach 38.6% of GDP.) Britain’s spending on debt interest has almost tripled since 2020.
Healey resigned as defense secretary under former Prime Minister Keir Starmer in June to protest the lack of military spending — but now faces mounting unanswered questions about his own plans.
Healey did two big new things on defense spending on Wednesday. First, he confirmed an open secret in Westminster: he plans to reach 3% of GDP by 2030 — on a path to NATO’s 3.5% by 2035 — but repeated that the details of how he’ll pay for it will only be spelled out in next year’s spending review.
Secondly and more significantly, he outlined his plan to plug a ​​£1.8 billion-a-year gap in Starmer’s defense investment plan — but provided only scant details.
The Treasury said it will be paid for by shaving 1% off each Whitehall department’s capital budget in the coming years. However, those departments have not yet worked out what they will cut; that is a problem for another day. These questions will dog Healey for the next year.
At least one person was delighted: Volodymyr Zelenskyy. The Ukrainian president said the chancellor “made my day” with a £10 billion package of economic and military support to Kyiv. Part of the package needed special sign-off by ministers because civil servants warned they could not guarantee it would provide value for money .
Much of what Healey did unveil appeared to be aimed at preserving the “Burnham bounce” in the polls and with his own MPs.
The chancellor called it a “budget for the working people of Britain” and Treasury analysis says it was redistributive, handing the biggest boost to the poorest households (albeit only raising their incomes by 0.6%).
Central to this was Healey’s closest thing to a “rabbit out of the hat” — a £100-per-household cash payment to people living in homes below a certain value this winter. One Labour MP enthused that the criteria for the payment (which Treasury officials say will capture 88% of the poorest households) was “absolutely brilliant” because it will capture working households and those on benefits at the same time.
There was another £1.5 billion for social and affordable housing, a “covenant” to govern new AI data centers and changes to mileage rates for self-employe

articles.title_orig: Spain Train Crash Live Updates: At Least 68 Killed in High-Speed Train Collision, Officials Say
articles.title_zh: Spain Train Crash Live Updates: At Least 68 Killed in High-Speed Train Collision, Officials Say
articles.content_orig:
Toledo, Spain 6:07 p.m. Oct. 28
A high-speed passenger train rear-ended another in Spain on Wednesday morning near the central city of Toledo, killing at least 68 people and injuring dozens more, officials said, in one of the deadliest train crashes in Spanish history.
The cause of the crash, which sent parts of both trains down a rural embankment, was not immediately clear. It was the second lethal crash this year involving the same two rail operators, and it was likely to deepen doubts about the security of Spain’s once-vaunted rail system.
In Spanish news reports, passengers described an awful impact that tossed people from a dining car, broke limbs and piled passengers atop one another. People crawled out of windows and lay in a nearby field, where local workers, who had heard the crash, rushed to help them with first aid kits and saw the first bodies.
The crash also came about a month ahead of national elections, and it had the potential to become an issue in an already bitter campaign about the competence of Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez’s left-wing government.
Sixty-eight people were seriously injured in the crash, 15 of them critically, said Emiliano García-Page, the president of the Castilla-La Mancha region.
Spain’s rail authority, the Adif, said the trains involved were a “Renfe train and another from the Iryo company,” both covering the route between Madrid, the capital, and the southern city of Seville. Renfe is the national rail provider.
Initial reports suggested that the Iryo train was stopped on the tracks, and that the Renfe train barreled into it. Local news outlets reported that there were 397 passengers aboard the Renfe train and about 150 aboard the Iryo train.
Trains from the same operators collided on a southern line in January, leaving 46 people dead.
Isaac Barrientos, a spokesman for the government’s transportation ministry, said on Wednesday that initial reports indicated two carriages of the Iryo train had derailed. He said all traffic on the Madrid-Andalusia route had been suspended until further notice.
Mr. Sánchez visited the scene of the crash on Wednesday afternoon, saying that Spanish rail’s security systems clearly needed to be reinforced. “If there has been negligence, it will come to light,” he said. “If there have been failures in the safety system, we will respond with the utmost firmness.” He declared three days of official mourning.
The conservative opposition leader, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, quickly voiced his own concern.
“I am very concerned about the information we are receiving regarding another train accident,” he wrote on social media soon after the crash. “The priority now is to assist the victims and support their families. My full support goes to the emergency teams working on the ground.” His Popular Party canceled all its campaign events around the country.
Another deadly crash: In January , a northbound Iryo train derailed, two of its cars falling onto the opposite track, and a southbound Renfe train slammed into the carriages seconds later. An official report on what caused that lethal accident has not been released, but preliminary investigations pointed to a broken rail as the likely cause.
A detailed account: In a news conference, Spain’s transportation minister described the events that he said preceded the crash on Wednesday.
José Bautista contributed reporting from the scene of the crash.
The U.S. State Department said in a statement that several U.S. citizens were among those injured in the crash. It did not provide information about their conditions.
Spain’s transportation minister said a train crash that killed dozens on Wednesday appeared to result from an “inexplicable” decision by traffic control operators to tell a high-speed train to continue its journey when another train was stopped farther along the tracks.
The minister, Óscar Puente, said he spent the morning watching a reconstruction of the accident and listening to audio recordings of communications between the control center in Madrid and the trains that crashed near Toledo, and he gave a detailed account of what he said preceded the crash at a news conference.
At about 8:30 a.m. local time, an automatic train control system near the site of the crash went down because of a computer failure, Mr. Puente said.
The system — known as the Linienzugbeeinflussung or LZB — dates to the 1960s and uses external technologies, such as track circuits and axel counters, to monitor the speed and position of trains. This information allows the system to automatically calculate when and how quickly a train can safely move forward. It then changes railroad signals accordingly.
On Wednesday, the safety system was inactive along a stretch of about 39 miles, or 63 kilometers, of tracks, so six trains traveling along that section were automatically stopped as a precaution. At that point, he said, the control center in Madrid took over.
“The control center communicated with the trains that had stopped, and at 8:36 a.m., the decision was made to allow the train that eventually collided with the stationary Iryo train to resume its journey as normal,” Mr. Puente said, referring to the private rail operator of the stopped train.
Traffic controllers working for Adif, the state-owned company that manages Spain’s rail infrastructure, told the train that eventually rear-ended the other to restart its planned journey, Mr. Puente said, “despite there being another train ahead of it.”
The train that was hit from behind was believed to have received instructions from traffic operators to continue, he said, but for unknown reasons it did not proceed.
The moving train then hit the stationary train.
“And that is the origin of the accident that has taken place,” Mr. Puente said, adding that the moving train should have been stopped according to protocol.
The Madrid-Seville route is currently undergoing a modernization program that will replace the LZB system with the more modern European Rail Traffic Management System. Infrastructure officials hope that the new system will cut down on human error in signaling.
Mr. Puente also said that the driver of an uninvolved train tried to warn the control center of the dangers when its operators greenlit the rear train’s resumption of its journey. That driver told the control center operator that trains should proceed at lower-than-normal speeds. The operator, Mr. Puente said, acknowledged his error. “Oh, yes,” the operator replied.
K. R. Callaway contributed reporting.
When the crash happened, Yahadi Mohamed Maulud, 41, who lives in the nearby town of Yébenes, loaded his car with water bottles and rushed to help. “We found a massacre,” he said, describing torn limbs and a blood-covered woman searching for her brother. One of the first to arrive at the scene, he helped to move injured passengers and carry stretchers. Mr. Maulud said he often took the train himself to Madrid for business, but no more: “I’m never getting on that train again.”
So many people showed up at Madrid hospitals on Wednesday to donate blood for victims of the train crash that the authorities are asking citizens to wait until Thursday or the following days, when more donations will be needed.
“The response from the people of Madrid to the call for blood donations is overwhelming,” said Isabel Díaz Ayuso, Madrid’s regional president. “Thank you, everyone.”
Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez spoke from the scene of the crash on Wednesday afternoon. “It’s not possible for a country like Spain to suffer two high-speed train accidents in one year,” he said, adding that while today’s accident and a fatal January crash on the same line seemed unrelated, Spanish rail’s security systems clearly needed to be reinforced.
“If there has been negligence, it will come to light,” he said. “If there have been failures in the safety system, we will respond with the utmost firmness.” Spain needs to understand “what is the origin of this tragedy,” he said.

articles.title_orig: Chinese astronomers find planets that somehow avoided death by red giant stars
articles.title_zh: Chinese astronomers find planets that somehow avoided death by red giant stars
articles.content_orig:
Study suggests the long-term fate of the solar system, including Earth, ‘may be far more complicated than predicted’, according to scientist
When a star like our sun grows old, it puffs up into a red giant that can gobble up its nearest planets.
But Chinese astronomers say they have found three solar systems where planets should have been eaten this way yet somehow survived – a puzzle that could change how scientists picture Earth’s distant future.
Using Nasa’s TESS space telescope, a team led by Qian Shengbang from Yunnan University showed that three Jupiter-like planets – each hugging an ageing star in the northern sky – had lived through their hosts ballooning out past them before shrinking back.

The leader of a Weil Gotshal & Manges practice group told his junior lawyers to look for employment, underscoring the firmâs perilous state as it consults with a restructuring lawyer.
Alex Lynch, who leads Weilâs capital markets group, communicated the news to associates in a group meeting Tuesday, a person familiar with the announcement said. He said the associates will remain employed for the time being and will continue to work on client matters, though he offered no specific timeline on their tenure, said the person, who requested anonymity to describe Weil communications.
Lynch and Weil did not respond to a request for comment.
The firmâs future existence is uncertain after a litany of partners fled, at least in part because of a lack of confidence in Weilâs leaders. Last month powerful corporate department chairman Michael Aiello moved toward an exit for rival Cravath, and a wide set of firm partners learned last weekend that incoming Weil leader Ramona Nee has decided not to take the job.
Davis Polk & Wardwell lawyers, including restructuring partner Brian Resnick, are advising Weil as it assesses its future, two people familiar with the matter said Tuesday. Resnick is head of Davis Polkâs liability management and special opportunities practice.
The storied New York-based firm, with more than 1,200 lawyers and $2 billion in revenue, has long been one of the USâs premier legal operations. It is renowned for its bankruptcy practice, acting as lead debtors counsel to Lehman Brothers Holdings Inc and Enron Corporation . It also was an M&A powerhouse, led by Aiello, who represented Fox Corp. on its $22 billion acquisition of Roku Inc.
Aielloâs departure along with others prompted the firm to explore its options, including a possible merger with another Big Law firm. But merger talks with Willkie Farr & Gallagher fell through last week, raising questions as to whether a dissolution is the inevitable option.

Content warning: this article contains references to allegations of sexual abuse which some readers might find distressing
Russell Brand has denied all the allegations made against him as he took to the witness box to give evidence in his trial at Southwark crown court.
The comedian, 51, told the court that his “entire life has been consumed by these allegations”.
Brand said he struggled to find anyone to give evidence on his behalf, saying the consequences of the September 2023 investigation by the Sunday Times, Times, and Channel 4 Dispatches were “devastating”.
He told jurors that he believed consent was “fundamental, essential, necessary and, indeed, in many ways more important than sex itself”.
During cross-examination, Brand admitted he was “obsessed” with sex in his younger years but denied being unable to function without it.
He denied the accusation that he would pretend to be gay to make women trust him.

The court is taking a 20 minute break.

articles.title_orig: ‘Noah’s Ark remains’ found burned and buried 30 feet below final resting place: report
articles.title_zh: ‘Noah’s Ark remains’ found burned and buried 30 feet below final resting place: report
articles.content_orig:
DOĞUBAYAZIT, Türkiye and VERO BEACH, Fla., Oct.  27, 2026  (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Mountains of Ararat -- Two weekends ago, researchers and officials gathered in eastern Turkey for the Noah’s Ark Symposium, where significant new findings from the 2026 study of the Durupınar Formation were presented. Prof. Dr. Cenker Atila of Sivas Cumhuriyet University, the lead archaeological professor overseeing the officially permitted project, reviewed and confirmed the preliminary results of advanced radar scans conducted by Dr. Khosrow Bakhtar. These results are now recognized as an official new development and finding of the Noah’s Ark 2026 Study.
Dr. Bakhtar explains an anomaly found by BakhtarRadar.
Dr. Bakhtar, a veteran U.S. defense scientist and inventor of the BakhtarRadar system used at the Durupinar site, reported detecting organized patterns, chambers, and corridors inside the roughly 515-foot-long, boat-shaped formation near the Mountains of Ararat. Critically, he stated that the features are not geological. Because the radar was configured to mask natural geological signals, any purely natural rock or soil anomaly would not have appeared in the processed imagery at all.
“This is the most significant finding of 45 years of my career. It’s not geologic related, because we masked all the geologic features,” Dr. Bakhtar said.
For many Americans familiar with the biblical account, the location and shape of the formation have long invited comparison with the vessel described in Genesis. Scripture records that the ark came to rest upon the mountains of Ararat (Genesis 8:4). The 2026 work, conducted under Sivas Cumhuriyet University and government authorization, represents the most extensive scientific examination of the site to date, combining radar, mapping, soil sampling, and core drilling. Prof. Dr. Cenker Atila also confirmed at the symposium that whatever lies beneath the surface of the Durupinar site has three “layers”.
“In our Holy Books, Noah’s Ark had three levels, in our radar studies, we also identified a formation with three levels” Dr. Cenker Atila told the media at the Noah’s Ark Symposium last week. - Dr. Cenker Atila told the media at the Noah’s Ark Symposium
Dr. Cenker Atila Speaks to Media at the Noah’s Ark Symposium
In a third major development announced by Prof. Dr. Atila, pieces of charred and burnt wood have been recovered from deep within the formation almost 30 feet down. The wood has been sent for carbon-14 dating and species identification. Researchers emphasize that no firm conclusions should be drawn until the laboratory results are complete and published.
What can be stated is that the material is not recent surface debris, or relocated from another region after being carried with mudflow; The wood was recovered from deep within the formation.
Coredrilling hole at the Durupinar Formation during the Noah’s Ark 2026 project
The charred condition of the wood is of particular interest. Scripture states that Noah was instructed to coat the ark “within and without with pitch” (Genesis 6:14). Natural pitch and tree resins are rich in flammable hydrocarbons they ignite easily. It’s possible that someone tried to set fire to the ark a long time ago, or it’s possible the wood became charred from lightning or volcanic activity in the region, also very long ago. Importantly, charring dramatically slows decomposition in soil, often to rates well under 1% per year.
It’s possible that what was meant to desecrate the ark may have instead been the very thing that preserved it.
Founder of Noah’s Ark Scans and Vice President of the Project Andrew Jones stated: “ It’s very exciting, but people need to understand that yes, it is possible that we have found the charred remains of Noah’s Ark, but it’s also possible that we have found the charred remains of a shepherd's campfire that he unwittingly decided to start while using the ark for shelter centuries ago” Andrew went on, “ We won’t know the exact age of the wood until carbon-14 and other testing is complete.”
Dr. Atila has indicated that photographs of the recovered charred wood will be released to the public in the near future. The project continues laboratory analysis of hundreds of soil and core samples, with further radar processing and reporting expected in the coming months. The team stresses that the work remains ongoing and that physical dating and material identification are essential next steps.
These developments add concrete, testable data to a site that has drawn interest from scientists, historians, and people of faith for more than six decades. For American Christians and others who take the biblical narrative seriously, the combination of subsurface structure consistent with organized internal features and the recovery of deep, charred wood represents a noteworthy advance in the historic investigation while still awaiting the decisive laboratory results that science requires.

US-listed shares of SK Hynix ( SKHY ) rose more than 9% on Wednesday after the memory maker's record profit and revenue quelled investor worries over the AI trade.
South Korean SK Hynix stock ( 000660.KS ) jumped 10%, while peer Samsung Electronics ( 005930.KS ) gained 9%. US-based Micron ( MU ) also rose 4%.
The South Korea-based company reported a 328% jump in quarterly revenue to roughly $78.7 billion, while operating profit surged 632% to about $62.7 billion, delivering an 80% operating margin. Meanwhile, quarter-over-quarter revenue and operating profit increased by 32% and 38%, respectively.
Growth was driven by surging AI data center demand, higher memory prices, and early shipments of HBM4, which SK Hynix expects to replace HBM3E as its mainstream product.
SK Hynix said more than 50% of its 2027-2028 capacity is already committed under long-term agreements. It reiterated that the AI memory shortage will persist through 2030 as adoption expands beyond cloud providers to enterprises and physical AI applications, including robotics and autonomous driving.
Wall Street remains bullish on memory demand. Now in its 14th quarter, the current chip boom has far outlasted historical cycles, which typically lasted eight to nine quarters.
RBC Capital Markets analyst Srini Pajjuri sees a credible path for the cycle to extend another five quarters.
"Robust AI demand, coupled with a shift toward memory-intensive agentic AI, continues to outpace supply, which is constrained by structural headwinds," Pajjuri wrote on Monday.
SK Hynix said it is returning an additional $45 billion to shareholders, bringing the total buybacks and dividends to an unprecedented $75.2 billion this year.
SK Hynix has been one of this year's highfliers. The company, which operates out of South Korea and trades on the Kospi ( ^KS11 ), listed on the Nasdaq earlier this year.
US-listed shares were trading near their IPO price following bouts of volatility in July and earlier this month. Last week, the company shelved plans for a US listing of its Solidigm flash memory unit after facing opposition from regulators and shareholders.
Ines Ferre is a Senior Business Reporter for Yahoo Finance covering the US stock market, publicly traded companies, and commodities.

articles.title_orig: Wife 'felt stranger's hand' during sex, court told
articles.title_zh: Wife 'felt stranger's hand' during sex, court told
articles.content_orig:
A woman said she locked herself in a bathroom after realising her then-husband had allowed someone else in the bedroom while she was blindfolded and having sex, a jury has heard.
In a police interview played at Winchester Crown Court, Joanne Young said she was restrained when she felt a hand on her wrist which she believed did not belong to her now ex-husband Philip Young.
Joanne - who has waived her legal right to anonymity - said Young, who has admitted drugging and raping her, later apologised and told her he had invited someone to watch the couple have sex after browsing online forums.
Four men who Young is alleged to have recruited to abuse his wife at their home are now on trial.
Warning: This story contains distressing details
On the second day of the four men's trial, two police interviews with Joanne were played to the court.
During the first interview, dated 29 July 2024, Joanne said the incident when she hid in the bathroom had happened in February 2023 after a night out with friends.
She told police she could not "remember all of it", but said Young had come upstairs after she had gone to bed.
Joanne said she "woke up with a blindfold and restraints on" and loosened the restraint on her right hand and then the left. At that point, she said, she felt a hand grip her wrist.
She said Young - who she believed was at the end of the bed - said "get down" to someone as she tried to take her blindfold off.
Joanne said she then saw someone ducking at the end of the bed and she ran to the bathroom and locked the door.
"The bed is a really big bed. So to have someone on the end of the bed and the left was not possible… I knew immediately," she told police.
The jury heard the couple discussed the incident, with Joanne telling police it was the first time she had ever seen her then-husband cry.
Joanne said she asked Young if he had ever invited anyone to watch them have sex before, which he denied.
"It was so intrusive. I was so upset. He knows I would have never said yes to that," she told police.
Joanne told the officer: "I didn't know if I should stay in the relationship or get myself out of the situation."
She said she took the incident as a "one-off" and tried to "move on".
Asked by an officer if there was a discussion between Young and Joanne about having someone else in the relationship, she said: "There was a joke years ago, a bit of banter, where he said in the kitchen something like 'would you ever want to sleep with someone else?'.
"I said no, and he said 'as long as I can watch you'. We laughed it off but it was a no."
She added: "It was never a part of our relationship. There'd never been a discussion. He never asked me what I wanted, it wasn't a conversation."
On the day Young was arrested, Joanne said he admitted to her he had shared images of her online without her consent.
Joanne said it had felt like a "kick in the stomach" and she was left in "shock and utter confusion".
She said: "How he could do that to me. How he could do something that's so intimate that's not allowed. How can he do it? How can you do that and think that was OK?"
The prosecution also read out statements from people who had been friends with Joanne and Young during their marriage.
Joanne's friend Susan said she thought the couple had a "dream relationship" before Joanne told her about the alleged incident of February 2023.
"She was in a real dark place about what happened," the statement said.
"After telling me, life went back to normal but what I witnessed from Jo was she didn't seem herself and that Phil had crossed a line from what he had done.
"Jo explained she was torn about why would Phil do this to her. She was in shock and seemed to be numb."
Emma Brown, who the court was told had been best friends with the couple since 2009, said Young "could handle his drink" and she "never saw him noticeably drunk".
"He was always on his mobile phone... I didn't know what he was doing as I didn't look at it," she added.
The four men jointly charged with Young, 50, are accused of the following offences:
Jurors were shown videos earlier which allegedly showed Sanderson-Doyle, Wilkins and Macksoni sexually assaulting Joanne.
Young, a former Conservative Swindon councillor, previously admitted 14 counts of voyeurism, 11 of rape, 11 of administering a substance with intent, seven of assault by penetration, four of sexual assault and one of publishing an obscene article.
He also published more than 500 intimate images and videos of his ex-wife and recorded her doing private acts for his own sexual gratification without her consent between 2010 and 2024.
A sixth defendant, Dean Hamilton, 47, of Street, Somerset, has admitted one charge of assault by penetration, two of sexual assault and one of rape.
Young and Hamilton will be sentenced at the end of the trial, which is expected to last up to four weeks.

articles.title_orig: Microsoft will post earnings after the bell amid job cuts and new cash-flow test
articles.title_zh: Microsoft will post earnings after the bell amid job cuts and new cash-flow test
articles.content_orig:
Microsoft shares rose 4% in extended trading on Wednesday after the company reported better-than-expected quarterly results, driven by 48% growth in its Azure cloud infrastructure business.
Here's how the company fared relative to LSEG consensus:
Microsoft's revenue grew 19% year over year in the quarter, which ended on Sept. 30, according to a statement , with Azure now its biggest single business.
The software giant has been rapidly building out data center infrastructure to meet artificial intelligence demand, while also maintaining positive free cash flow unlike its fellow hyperscalers. Microsoft reported  $45.2 billion worth of capital expenditures and finance leases during the quarter, up about 30% from a year earlier. Analysts surveyed by StreetAccount had projected $50.67 billion.
Microsoft flagged a higher growth rate for cash paid for property and equipment than overall capital expenditures, which include finance leases, because of "timing differences between receipt of goods and payment and a lower mix of finance leases."
Free cash flow declined 27% to $18.63 billion. Cloud rival Alphabet reported more than $9 billion in negative free cash flow in the quarter after Meta said last week its cash flow turned negative for the first time.
Microsoft's net income increased to $36.63 billion, or $4.92 per share, from $27.75 billion, or $3.72 per share, a year ago. Adjusted earnings exclude a roughly $200 million impact from its investment in OpenAI.
For the first time, Microsoft disclosed revenue from its Azure cloud in dollars, at $33.17 billion in the quarter. Analysts polled by StreetAccount expected $32.32 billion. The growth rate in the June quarter was 42%.
Microsoft reported results under two operating segments — Agents and Infra, and Devices and Consumer.  For the past 11 years, the company had three segments that divided up its Azure, Office and Windows businesses.
In Agents and Infra, revenue rose almost 25% to $76.8 billion, more than the $75.63 billion consensus among analysts polled by StreetAccount. The segment contains Azure, along with Microsoft 365 cloud products, productivity and server licensing, industry solutions and frontier and support services.
Revenue in the Devices and Consumer business slipped 3% to $15.48 billion, beating the StreetAccount consensus of $15.05 billion. The unit includes search and advertising, Xbox, devices and Windows operating system licenses sold to device makers.
Sales of devices and Windows licenses declined 22%, as higher memory and storage costs elevated prices.
As of Wednesday's close, Microsoft shares were up about 10% year to date, trailing the S&P 500 index, which has gained 13% over the same period.
During the fiscal first quarter, Microsoft said it would cut 4,800 jobs , and followed up by announcing on Monday that it's offering buyouts to up to 60,000 employees, as it strives to balance a costly AI build-out with capital efficiency. Microsoft also established, during the quarter, an AI implementation unit and revealed a Copilot AI "super app" with coding abilities.
This story is developing. Please check back for updates.
